This document is the R counterpart of the Python notebook
[Part 02 - Searching and Snowballing](../../Notebooks/Part%2002%20-%20Searching%20and%20Snowballing/Part%2002%20-%20Searching%20and%20Snowballing.ipynb).
Part 01 archived one account we chose in advance. This part builds a
*topical* archive when we don't know in advance whose posts matter, by
two complementary routes: keyword search, and snowball sampling along the
mention and reply ties embedded in posts.

### Learning objectives

* Query `app.bsky.feed.searchPosts` with date, language, and tag filters.
* Read the anatomy of a post record, especially its *facets*.
* Implement snowball sampling over mention and reply-parent edges.
* Diagnose saturation: when does another wave stop adding new material?
* Assemble, deduplicate, and persist a documented post archive.

## Setup

```{r libraries}
library(bskyr)
library(tidyverse)
library(jsonlite)
library(lubridate)
```

As in every part of this series, the shared helper `bsky_client.R` looks
for credentials (an `atproto.json` file or bskyr's environment
variables), authenticates if it finds them, and sets `bsky_authed`. The
`knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)` line then makes that flag the
default for the whole document: with credentials every chunk runs;
without them the document still knits, but the API chunks are skipped.

```{r connect}
source("bsky_client.R")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = bsky_authed)
```

One difference from the Python series is worth flagging immediately: in
Python, search is the *one* endpoint in this part that demands
authentication (the public AppView returns 403 for it). bskyr
authenticates every call, so when this document runs at all, search runs
too.

## 1. Searching for posts

[`bs_search_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_search_posts.html) wraps `app.bsky.feed.searchPosts`. A quoted phrase
matches exactly; `since`/`until`, `lang`, and `tag` narrow the window.

Search results come back shaped a little differently from author feeds:
the author isn't spread across `author_*` columns but kept whole in a
list-column called `author`, one small tibble per post. We reach into it
with the same `map_chr()` idiom we use on `record`:

```{r search-basic}
hits <- bs_search_posts('"snowball sampling"', limit = 5)

hits |>
  mutate(author_handle = map_chr(author, "handle"),
         text = map_chr(record, "text", .default = NA)) |>
  select(author_handle, text)
```

### Paginating a search

Like every list endpoint, search paginates with cursors, and bskyr
follows them automatically when `limit > 100`. Here are the last seven
days of English-language posts tagged `#openscience`:

```{r search-paged}
until <- now("UTC")
since <- until - days(7)

results <- bs_search_posts(
  "#openscience",
  since = format(since, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
  until = format(until, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ"),
  lang  = "en",
  sort  = "latest",
  limit = 300
)

c(posts = nrow(results), accounts = n_distinct(map_chr(results$author, "did")))
```

### When you cannot search

Search indexes only what the index operator chooses to index, ranks
results opaquely, and (on some platforms) disappears entirely. The
snowball design in Section 4 builds a topical archive from *public graph
structure alone* — a strategy that survives even when search does not.

## 2. The anatomy of a post record

Endpoints like [`bs_get_author_feed()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_author_feed.html)
and [`bs_get_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_posts.html)
return hydrated **post views**. Two layers matter:

* The **record** is what the author's repository actually stores: the
  text, creation time, language tags, reply references, facets, and
  embeds. This is the durable, author-controlled part. In bskyr's cleaned
  tibbles it is the `record` list-column.
* The **view** wraps the record with AppView-computed context: the
  author's profile, like/repost/reply counts, and hydrated embeds. This
  part changes every time you fetch.

Every post is identified by two values you will see everywhere in AT
Protocol data:

* Its **URI** is the post's address, written in the
  [`at://` scheme](https://atproto.com/specs/at-uri-scheme):
  `at://<DID>/<collection>/<record key>`. The **DID**
  ([decentralized identifier](https://atproto.com/specs/did)) is the
  account's permanent machine ID. Unlike a handle, it never changes even
  if the user renames themselves, which is why researchers should key
  datasets on DIDs. The collection (`app.bsky.feed.post`) says what kind
  of record this is, and the [record key](https://atproto.com/specs/record-key)
  is a short, timestamp-flavored ID for this particular post.
* Its **CID** (content identifier) is a cryptographic fingerprint (hash)
  of the record's content. Where the URI says "the post at this address",
  the CID says "exactly this version of it"; together they form a
  *strong reference* that cannot be silently swapped for different
  content.

Rather than pinning one post by its URI (live posts can be deleted at
any time, which would break the document), we scan the recent posts of
the series' two standing accounts, `nytimes.com` and `bsky.app`, and
pick the original post that uses the most *kinds* of facet (mentions,
hashtags, links; the Facets subsection below explains them), newest first
among ties. Institutional accounts rarely use all three in one post, so
expect one or two kinds. `n_feature_types()` collects every feature's
`$type` in a record and counts the distinct ones:

```{r record-anatomy}
n_feature_types <- function(record) {
  types <- unlist(map(record$facets[[1]], \(facet) map_chr(facet$features, "$type")))
  length(unique(types))
}

recent_originals <- function(actor) {
  feed <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, limit = 100)
  Sys.sleep(0.1)
  feed[!is_repost(feed), ] |>
    transmute(uri, author_handle, record,
              n_types = map_int(record, n_feature_types),
              created = map_chr(record, "created_at", .default = NA))
}

example <- bind_rows(recent_originals("nytimes.com"), recent_originals("bsky.app")) |>
  arrange(desc(n_types), desc(created)) |>
  slice_head(n = 1)

example |> select(author_handle, n_types)
example |> mutate(text = map_chr(record, "text")) |> pull(text)
```

### Facets

Mentions, hashtags, and links are not parsed out of the text by clients —
they are declared by the author's client as **facets**: byte ranges of
the text paired with typed *features*. Inspect the example post's facets:

```{r facets}
facets <- example$record[[1]]$facets[[1]]

str(facets, max.level = 3, list.len = 4)
```

Each feature's `$type` ends in `#mention` (with a `did`), `#tag` (with a
`tag`), or `#link` (with a full `uri`, even when the visible text was
shortened for display). This is wonderful for researchers: mentions
arrive pre-resolved to DIDs (no fragile handle parsing), and links
arrive un-shortened. Because mentions carry DIDs, stable account
identifiers, facets turn a pile of text into a *network*.

Each facet's `index` gives `byteStart` and `byteEnd`, offsets into the
**UTF-8 encoded bytes** of the text, *not* character positions. The
distinction matters the moment a post contains an emoji or a non-Latin
script, where one character can occupy several bytes. To recover the
highlighted span, convert the text to bytes with `charToRaw()`, slice the
bytes, and convert back. (R vectors count from 1 and include both ends,
so the slice is `byteStart + 1` through `byteEnd`.)

```{r facet-spans}
example_text <- example$record[[1]]$text
text_bytes <- charToRaw(enc2utf8(example_text))

map(facets, \(facet) {
  span <- rawToChar(text_bytes[(facet$index$byteStart + 1):facet$index$byteEnd])
  Encoding(span) <- "UTF-8"
  feature <- facet$features[[1]]
  tibble(kind = sub(".*#", "", feature$`$type`),
         span = span,
         target = feature$did %||% feature$tag %||% feature$uri)
}) |>
  list_rbind()
```

Each row pairs a highlighted span of the visible text with the
machine-readable target stored behind it. This is exactly the structure
the helpers in the next section rely on: no regular expressions, no
guessing.

### Languages, replies, and embeds

Three more record fields we use when building the archive:

* **`langs`**: a list of self-declared language codes. These are set by
  the posting client (often auto-detected, sometimes wrong), so treat
  them as a useful filter, not ground truth.
* **`reply`**: present when the post is a reply, containing **strong
  references** (URI + CID pairs, as defined above) to the *parent* post
  (the post being answered) and the thread *root* (the post that started
  the thread). The parent's author DID is embedded right inside the
  `at://` URI, which we exploit for snowballing.
* **`embed`**: attached media: images, video, an external link card, or
  a quoted post. The record stores the author's intent (for example
  `app.bsky.embed.external`), while the view carries the hydrated
  version with resolved thumbnails. Part 07 is devoted to these.

```{r record-fields}
example_record <- example$record[[1]]

list(
  langs = unlist(example_record$langs),
  is_reply = !is.null(example_record$reply),   # our example is an original post
  record_embed = example_record$embed[[1]]$`$type` %||% "(none)"
)
```

## 3. Facet helpers

Three small functions pull the network out of a feed tibble; they are
this part's equivalent of the Python `snowball.py` module. The logic of
`extract_features()`: a record's `facets` element is a list of facets,
each facet holds a list of features, and each feature has a `$type`
ending in `#mention`, `#tag`, or `#link`. We walk that nesting with two
layers of `map()`, keep the features whose type matches, and pull out
the field we want (`did` for mentions, `tag` for hashtags, `uri` for
links). `discard(..., is.na)` then drops the non-matches:

```{r helpers}
extract_features <- function(record, feature_type, field) {
  facets <- record$facets[[1]]
  if (is.null(facets)) return(character(0))
  out <- map(facets, \(facet) {
    map_chr(facet$features, \(feature) {
      if (endsWith(feature$`$type`, feature_type)) feature[[field]]
      else NA_character_
    })
  })
  discard(unlist(out), is.na)
}

extract_mentions <- function(record) extract_features(record, "#mention", "did")
extract_tags     <- function(record) extract_features(record, "#tag", "tag")
extract_links    <- function(record) extract_features(record, "#link", "uri")

list(
  mentions = extract_mentions(example_record),
  hashtags = extract_tags(example_record),
  links    = extract_links(example_record)
)
```

## 4. Snowball sampling: from one seed to a corpus

Snowball sampling starts from a *seed*, observes whom the seed engages,
collects those accounts, and repeats. Set the design parameters first —
every cap is a promise to the API and to your own time:

Each value mirrors the constant of the same name in the Python
notebook's Section 4, so the two implementations run the same design:

```{r params}
SEED_ACTOR         <- "nytimes.com"
WAVE0_MAX_POSTS    <- 200  # posts to collect from the seed
WAVE1_ACCOUNTS     <- 8    # most-engaged accounts to crawl in wave 1
POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT  <- 100  # posts per snowballed account
MAX_TOTAL_ACCOUNTS <- 15   # hard cap across all waves
MAX_PAGES          <- 10   # feed pages per account (Python: fetch_author_posts max_pages=10)

COLLECTED_AT <- format(now("UTC"), "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ")
COLLECTED_AT
```

### Wave 0: the seed account

A small fetcher that returns up to `max_posts` original posts (reposts
dropped) with the columns the snowball needs. It pages through the feed
100 items at a time, the same way the Python helper does, because
asking bskyr for `limit = max_posts` items would count reposts toward
the limit: an account that reposts heavily would come back with far
fewer original posts than we asked for. bskyr attaches the cursors it
received to the tibble it returns, as a list in `attr(feed, "cursor")`;
the last one tells the server where to resume, so we pass it back to
fetch the next page, stopping when we have enough originals, the cursor
runs out, or `MAX_PAGES` requests have been made.

Two of the columns come from the helpers in `bsky_client.R`, because
bskyr's raw column names are easy to get wrong in ways that fail
*silently*:

* `is_repost()` identifies reposts. We drop them, because a repost's
  text, mentions, and author belong to someone else. Getting this wrong
  would let other accounts' posts, and their DIDs, leak into each wave.
* `reply_parent_did()` gives the DID of the account each post replies to.
  On Bluesky, replies don't @-mention their parent, so without this the
  snowball would follow mentions only and miss every conversation.

```{r fetch-author}
originals_from_page <- function(feed) {
  feed |>
    mutate(
      repost     = is_repost(feed),
      text       = map_chr(record, "text", .default = NA),
      created_at = map_chr(record, "created_at", .default = NA),
      is_reply   = is_reply(feed),
      reply_parent_did = reply_parent_did(feed),
      mentions   = map(record, extract_mentions),
      hashtags   = map(record, extract_tags)
    ) |>
    filter(!repost) |>
    select(uri, author_did, author_handle, created_at, text, is_reply,
           reply_parent_did, mentions, hashtags,
           like_count, repost_count, reply_count)
}

fetch_author_posts <- function(actor, max_posts = 100, max_pages = MAX_PAGES) {
  pages <- list()
  cursor <- NULL
  for (page in seq_len(max_pages)) {
    feed <- bs_get_author_feed(actor, cursor = cursor, limit = 100)
    if (is.null(feed) || nrow(feed) == 0) break
    pages[[page]] <- originals_from_page(feed)
    cursor <- tail(unlist(attr(feed, "cursor")), 1)   # NULL once the feed runs out
    if (length(cursor) == 0 || sum(map_int(pages, nrow)) >= max_posts) break
    Sys.sleep(0.1)
  }
  list_rbind(pages) |> slice_head(n = max_posts)
}

wave0 <- fetch_author_posts(SEED_ACTOR, WAVE0_MAX_POSTS)
seed_did <- wave0$author_did[[1]]

c(posts = nrow(wave0))
range(wave0$created_at)
```

### Whom does the seed engage?

Whom did those posts engage? For each post we collect the accounts it
engages, its mentions plus the author of the post it replies to, and
then count, for each account, **how many posts** engaged it. Two details
match the Python helper `count_engaged_accounts()`. A post that mentions
someone three times still counts once for them (`unique()`), so the
tally measures how often an account is engaged, not how chatty one post
was. And we remove the post's own author (`setdiff()`), so an account
threading replies to itself doesn't count as engaging itself. `pmap()`
walks the three columns in parallel, one post at a time; `table()`
tallies the result, and we sort so the most-engaged accounts come first.
The top `WAVE1_ACCOUNTS` of them form the next wave's crawl list — note
that we exclude the seed itself, since we already have its posts:

```{r engaged}
count_engaged <- function(posts, exclude = character(0)) {
  engaged <- pmap(list(posts$mentions, posts$reply_parent_did, posts$author_did),
                  \(mentions, parent, author) {
    setdiff(unique(c(unlist(mentions), parent[!is.na(parent)])),
            c(author, exclude))
  })
  as.character(unlist(engaged)) |>
    table() |>
    sort(decreasing = TRUE)
}

engaged0 <- count_engaged(wave0, exclude = seed_did)
wave1_dids <- names(head(engaged0, WAVE1_ACCOUNTS))

if (length(wave1_dids) < WAVE1_ACCOUNTS) {
  cat("The design asked for", WAVE1_ACCOUNTS, "wave-1 accounts; wave 0 engaged only",
      length(wave1_dids), "so wave 1 crawls all of them.\n")
}

bs_get_profile(wave1_dids) |>
  mutate(posts_engaging = as.integer(engaged0[did])) |>
  select(handle, did, posts_engaging)
```

Compare the number of rows above with the design's `WAVE1_ACCOUNTS`. A
newsroom's posts are mostly headlines and links; it rarely replies to
anyone and mentions only a few accounts, mostly its own sister
publications. So the frontier can come out *smaller than the design
asked for*. That is a finding about the seed, not a bug: an
institutional account is a narrow doorway into the network, and if your
design depends on a wide first wave, you would add seeds rather than
quietly accept fewer accounts. The metadata file records both the
parameter and the accounts actually crawled.

### Wave 1: crawl the frontier

Now collect posts from each account on the crawl list. `crawl_accounts()`
calls our fetcher once per account, pausing between accounts, and wraps
each call in `tryCatch()`: an account that was deleted or suspended
since the seed mentioned it is skipped with a message naming it, rather
than stopping the whole crawl or vanishing without a trace:

```{r wave1}
crawl_accounts <- function(dids, posts_each) {
  map(dids, \(did) {
    posts <- tryCatch(fetch_author_posts(did, posts_each), error = function(e) {
      message("Skipping ", did, ": ", conditionMessage(e))
      NULL
    })
    Sys.sleep(0.1)
    posts
  }) |> list_rbind()
}

wave1 <- crawl_accounts(wave1_dids, POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT)
crawled <- c(seed_did, wave1_dids)

c(posts = nrow(wave1), accounts = length(wave1_dids))
```

### Wave 2: one more hop

```{r wave2}
engaged1 <- count_engaged(wave1, exclude = crawled)
budget <- MAX_TOTAL_ACCOUNTS - length(crawled)
wave2_dids <- names(head(engaged1, budget))

wave2 <- crawl_accounts(wave2_dids, POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT)
crawled <- c(crawled, wave2_dids)

c(posts = nrow(wave2), total_accounts_crawled = length(crawled))
```

### Where did the snowball go?

Before measuring saturation, look at *who* wave 2 recruited. Each wave-2
account was reached because some wave-1 account engaged it. The next
chunk credits every wave-2 account to the wave-1 account whose posts
engaged it most often, its **gateway** into the sample. For each wave-2
DID, it runs `count_engaged()` on each wave-1 post separately (one row
at a time), keeps the authors of the posts that engaged that DID, and
takes the most frequent one:

```{r gateway}
gateway_of <- function(did) {
  engaged_it <- map_lgl(seq_len(nrow(wave1)),
                        \(i) did %in% names(count_engaged(wave1[i, ])))
  authors <- wave1$author_handle[engaged_it]
  if (length(authors) == 0) return(NA_character_)
  names(sort(table(authors), decreasing = TRUE))[1]
}

tibble(gateway = map_chr(wave2_dids, gateway_of)) |>
  count(gateway, sort = TRUE)
```

If one wave-1 account is the gateway for most of wave 2, the snowball
has been **captured by one community**: it followed the densest cluster
of engagement out of the seed's neighborhood and spent the rest of its
budget there. With a newsroom seed this tends to happen through one
well-connected writer or sister publication with a large circle of
peers: a columnist whose replies and mentions lead to other
commentators, or a sports site whose writers constantly mention one
another. Run the document on different days and the gateway can change,
but the pattern recurs. Two biases are at work. **Homophily**: people
engage with others like themselves, so once the crawl enters a
community, every further wave stays inside it. **Popularity bias**:
ranking the frontier by engagement counts sends the budget to whoever
is mentioned most. Neither shows up in the saturation numbers below,
which is why you should always look at *who* a snowball reached as well
as *how much* it collected.

## 5. Saturation diagnostics: when to stop

Each wave should be judged by its *marginal yield*: how many genuinely
new posts, accounts, and hashtags it added. When the curves flatten, the
snowball has saturated the neighborhood of the seed.

One piece of R syntax to flag in the next chunk: the `<<-` operator
assigns to a variable *outside* the current function, which lets our
per-wave function update the running sets of already-seen posts,
accounts, and hashtags as `imap()` walks over the waves in order:

```{r saturation, fig.width=10, fig.height=3.5}
waves <- list(`0` = wave0, `1` = wave1, `2` = wave2)

seen_posts <- seen_accounts <- seen_tags <- character(0)
wave_stats <- imap(waves, \(posts, wave) {
  new_posts <- setdiff(posts$uri, seen_posts)
  accounts  <- unique(c(posts$author_did, unlist(posts$mentions),
                        discard(posts$reply_parent_did, is.na)))
  new_accounts <- setdiff(accounts, seen_accounts)
  tags <- unique(unlist(posts$hashtags))
  new_tags <- setdiff(tags, seen_tags)
  seen_posts    <<- c(seen_posts, new_posts)
  seen_accounts <<- c(seen_accounts, new_accounts)
  seen_tags     <<- c(seen_tags, new_tags)
  tibble(wave = wave, posts_collected = nrow(posts),
         new_posts = length(new_posts),
         new_accounts = length(new_accounts),
         new_hashtags = length(new_tags))
}) |> list_rbind()

wave_stats

wave_stats |>
  pivot_longer(starts_with("new_"), names_to = "yield") |>
  ggplot(aes(wave, value, fill = yield)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~yield, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Wave", y = "New per wave",
       title = "Marginal yield of each snowball wave") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## 6. Building the archive

Now assemble the deliverable. `list_rbind()` stacks the three waves into
one tibble (tagging each post with the wave that found it),
`distinct(uri, ...)` keeps only the first sighting of each post — the
same post can be collected twice when snowballed accounts reply to each
other — and `ymd_hms()` parses the timestamps:

```{r archive}
archive <- imap(waves, \(posts, wave) mutate(posts, wave = as.integer(wave))) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  distinct(uri, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(created_at = ymd_hms(created_at, quiet = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(created_at)

dim(archive)
```

### Saving the archive — and its provenance

List-columns (mentions, hashtags) don't fit CSV, so the full archive goes
to RDS and a flat projection to CSV; the metadata records every design
parameter:

```{r save-archive}
dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)

saveRDS(archive, "data/archive.rds")
archive |>
  mutate(across(c(mentions, hashtags),
                \(col) map_chr(col, paste, collapse = " "))) |>
  write_csv("data/archive.csv")

metadata <- list(
  collected_at = COLLECTED_AT,
  collection_method = "snowball sample over mention and reply-parent edges",
  seed_actor = SEED_ACTOR,
  seed_did = seed_did,
  parameters = list(
    wave0_max_posts = WAVE0_MAX_POSTS,
    wave1_accounts = WAVE1_ACCOUNTS,
    posts_per_account = POSTS_PER_ACCOUNT,
    max_total_accounts = MAX_TOTAL_ACCOUNTS,
    reposts_included = FALSE,
    replies_included = TRUE
  ),
  accounts_crawled = sort(crawled),
  total_posts = nrow(archive)
)
write_json(metadata, "data/archive_metadata.json",
           pretty = TRUE, auto_unbox = TRUE)
```

### Proving the round trip

```{r roundtrip}
reloaded <- readRDS("data/archive.rds")

stopifnot(nrow(reloaded) == nrow(archive),
          all(reloaded$uri == archive$uri))
c(posts = nrow(reloaded), authors = n_distinct(reloaded$author_did))
```

### Re-hydrating archived posts

Archives go stale: posts get deleted, counters keep moving. [`bs_get_posts()`](https://christophertkenny.com/bskyr/reference/bs_get_posts.html)
re-fetches a batch of URIs so you can measure attrition:

```{r rehydrate}
set.seed(42)
sample_uris <- sample(reloaded$uri, 10)

fresh <- bs_get_posts(sample_uris)

tibble(uri = sample_uris) |>
  left_join(select(fresh, uri, like_count_now = like_count), by = "uri") |>
  left_join(select(reloaded, uri, like_count), by = "uri") |>
  mutate(still_exists = !is.na(like_count_now)) |>
  select(like_count, like_count_now, still_exists)
```

## 7. A first look at the archive

Before any serious analysis, basic descriptives tell us what the snowball
actually scooped up, and they double as sanity checks on the collection
itself. Three quick views: the hashtag vocabulary, the most-mentioned
accounts, and how the corpus is distributed across authors.

First, hashtags. Because `hashtags` is a list-column, `unnest()` gives
every (post, hashtag) pair its own row, and `count()` tallies them. The
result is the archive's topical vocabulary at a glance:

```{r top-tags, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
archive |>
  select(hashtags) |>
  unnest(hashtags) |>
  count(hashtags, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 15) |>
  ggplot(aes(n, fct_reorder(hashtags, n))) +
  geom_col(fill = "seagreen") +
  labs(x = "Posts using hashtag", y = NULL,
       title = paste0("Top hashtags in the archive (n=", nrow(archive), " posts)")) +
  theme_minimal()
```

Second, the most-mentioned accounts. The `mentions` column stores DIDs,
stable but unreadable, so after the same unnest-and-count pattern we
resolve the top ten back to handles with a single batched
`bs_get_profile()` call (it accepts up to 25 actors). Mentioned accounts
can be deleted or deactivated by the time you look them up, so any DID
the call doesn't return is marked as unresolvable. The table is a rough
who's-who of the conversations the snowball traversed:

```{r top-mentions}
top_mentions <- archive |>
  select(mentions) |>
  unnest(mentions) |>
  count(mentions, sort = TRUE, name = "times_mentioned") |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  rename(did = mentions)

mentioned_profiles <- tryCatch(bs_get_profile(top_mentions$did),
                               error = \(e) tibble(did = character(), handle = character()))

top_mentions |>
  left_join(select(mentioned_profiles, did, handle), by = "did") |>
  mutate(handle = coalesce(handle, "(unresolvable)")) |>
  select(handle, did, times_mentioned)
```

Third, the shape of the corpus itself: how many posts each crawled
author contributed. Watch for imbalance here: if one prolific account
contributes a third of the archive, any "corpus-level" finding may
really be a finding about that one account.

```{r by-author, fig.width=8, fig.height=5}
by_author <- archive |>
  group_by(author_handle) |>
  summarise(posts = n(), replies = sum(is_reply),
            median_likes = median(like_count, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  arrange(desc(posts))

ggplot(by_author, aes(posts, fct_reorder(author_handle, posts))) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  labs(x = "Posts in archive", y = NULL,
       title = "Posts per author, by snowball account") +
  theme_minimal()

by_author
```

## 8. Research design: what kind of sample is this?

The descriptives above already show the sample's construction leaking
into its content: the top hashtags and most-mentioned accounts reflect
whom we chose to crawl at least as much as any underlying conversation.
A snowball sample is *defensible*, not *representative*. Before treating
an archive like this as "the conversation", name its biases:

* **Seed dependence.** Everything is anchored to one account's social
  neighborhood. A different seed yields a different corpus; serious
  designs use multiple, deliberately diverse seeds and report
  sensitivity to seed choice.
* **Popularity bias.** Ranking the frontier by engagement count
  systematically recruits visible, frequently mentioned accounts. Quiet
  participants in the same conversations are under-sampled, the same
  dynamic that makes hashtag samples over-represent the loudest voices
  (Tufekci 2014).
* **Homophily.** People engage with similar others, so waves stay inside
  communities resembling the seed and cross community boundaries slowly.
  Two waves from a newsroom seed yield a corpus of journalists and
  sister publications, whatever the topic, and the gateway table in
  Section 4 shows how far a single account can pull the whole sample.
* **Activity bias.** "Most recent N posts" covers different time windows
  for different accounts: a prolific poster's 100 posts span days, a
  quiet account's span years. Time-bounded designs should filter on
  `created_at` instead of post counts.
* **Index and survivorship effects.** Search-based frames (Section 1)
  inherit the index's gaps; snowball frames inherit deletion effects at
  collection time. Both differ from real-time collection (Part 10).

None of these are fatal: every sampling frame has biases. What separates
defensible from indefensible corpora is **documentation**: the seeds, the
edge definition, the caps, the stopping rule, and the collection date,
all written down before reviewers ask. That is the job of
`archive_metadata.json`, and it is the discipline Bruns & Burgess (2011)
urged when they showed that a "hashtag public" is an analytic
construction, not a natural object. Respondent-driven sampling
(Heckathorn 1997) shows how far the design can be pushed when you track
recruitment chains carefully; our `wave` column preserves exactly that
information. For a broad, readable catalogue of how these biases arise at
every stage of the social-data pipeline, see Olteanu et al. (2019).

## Ethics and limitations

**Third parties never opted in.** This is the central ethical fact of
snowball designs: the seed is a large institutional account, chosen
because a newsroom's public posting is its professional output, but the
individual journalists and other accounts pulled in by mentions and
replies made no such choice. Our archive contains their posts solely
because someone else engaged them. Minimize accordingly: collect only the
fields your question needs, prefer aggregates (as in Section 7) over
individual rows when reporting, and paraphrase rather than quote, since
verbatim post text is trivially re-identifiable via search even with
handles removed (the lesson of Zimmer 2010).

**Honor deletion and opt-out signals.** Users delete posts and accounts,
and some set the `!no-unauthenticated` label on their profiles. Record
collection dates (we did), re-check with `bs_get_posts()` before
re-publishing (Section 6), and drop records that have disappeared.

**Bots and automated accounts** ride along in mention-based frontiers:
inspect your crawl list before interpreting the corpus as human
conversation.

**Public is not consent, and exempt is not automatic.** Bluesky users
mostly have not read the protocol docs and may not expect their posts in
a dataset (Fiesler & Proferes 2018). Consult your IRB and the AoIR
Internet Research Ethics guidelines (franzke et al. 2020,
[PDF](https://aoir.org/reports/ethics3.pdf)) before turning a tutorial
pipeline into a study.

**Limitations of this archive.** It is demonstration-scale (at most
`MAX_TOTAL_ACCOUNTS` accounts and about a hundred posts from each; the
metadata file records the exact counts) and account-anchored rather than
topic-anchored; with search (Section 1) you would combine both to
triangulate a topical frame. Bluesky's user base skews toward early
adopters and Twitter migrants, so prevalence claims do not generalize
beyond the platform (Tufekci 2014).

## Exercises

These extend the document roughly in order of ambition. For all of them,
keep the politeness conventions (pauses between requests, explicit caps)
and write your design choices down the way `archive_metadata.json` does.

1. **Swap the seed.** Change `SEED_ACTOR` to `bsky.app` (the official
   Bluesky account) and re-run Sections 4–7. Which top hashtags and
   most-mentioned accounts change, and which crawl parameters did you
   have to adjust to stay under budget?
2. **Go one wave deeper.** Add a wave 3: rank the accounts wave 2
   engaged (excluding everyone already crawled), raise
   `MAX_TOTAL_ACCOUNTS` modestly (say, to 25), and extend the saturation
   table and charts. Do the discovery curves for new accounts and new
   hashtags bend downward, or is the frontier still expanding?
3. **Change the edge definition.** Modify the frontier ranking to use
   *mentions only*, then *reply parents only* (write two small variants
   of `count_engaged()`). How much do the two top-8 frontiers overlap
   with each other and with the original?
4. **Time-bound wave 0.** Replace "the most recent posts" with "every
   original post since a fixed date" by filtering on the record's
   `created_at` during collection. Section 8 explains why: fixed-window
   designs make accounts comparable in *time* rather than in post count.
5. **Compare two seeds' archives.** Build a second archive from a
   different seed (Exercise 1), save it under a different filename, and
   quantify how much the two corpora share: the
   [Jaccard similarity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaccard_index) of
   their author-DID sets and of their hashtag vocabularies, using
   `intersect()` and `union()` on the unnested columns.
6. **Hashtag co-occurrence network.** For every post with two or more
   hashtags, generate the tag pairs with `combn(tags, 2)`, count pairs,
   and inspect the top 20 as an edge list. For a preview of Part 03, load
   the edge list into igraph with `graph_from_data_frame()` and plot the
   network of tags that travel together.

## Research project ideas

**1. Who do hashtags miss? Auditing a hashtag public on Bluesky.** Bruns
& Burgess (2011) framed hashtags as "ad hoc publics", and Tufekci (2014)
warned that hashtag samples capture only the most performative
participants. *Question:* who participates in a conversation without ever
tagging it? *Data:* an authenticated `bs_search_posts()` archive for an
active hashtag over a fixed window, plus a snowball from 3–5 visibly
active participants over the same window. *Method:* find accounts in the
snowball corpus whose posts discuss the topic (keyword match in `text`)
but never carry the hashtag, and compare their posting and engagement
profiles to the hashtag users'. *Expected challenge:* deciding a post is
"about the topic" without the tag needs a keyword dictionary or a simple
classifier, validated by hand-coding a sample.

**2. Seed sensitivity: how fragile are snowball corpora?** Morstatter et
al. (2013) showed that conclusions can hinge on how a sample was drawn;
Olteanu et al. (2019) catalogue acquisition bias as a pipeline-wide
problem. *Question:* how much does a two-wave snowball corpus depend on
its seed? *Data:* the identical pipeline (same caps, edge definition and
date) run from five or more seeds in visibly different communities.
*Method:* pairwise Jaccard overlap of account sets and hashtag
vocabularies, then a test of which summary statistics (reply share,
median likes, top-tag concentration) are stable across seeds. *Expected
challenge:* budget; five crawls multiply the request count, so you need
Part 01's rate-limit discipline and tight per-account caps.

**3. The half-life of a post archive.** Archives inherit survivorship
bias (Morstatter et al. 2013), and deletion is an ethical signal you are
obliged to honor (Zimmer 2010; Fiesler & Proferes 2018). *Question:* how
fast does a Bluesky archive decay through deletion and engagement drift,
and is the decay selective? *Data:* one snowball archive, re-hydrated
weekly with `bs_get_posts()` (Section 6) for 8–12 weeks, storing only
per-URI status and counts. *Method:* a survival curve for deletion, a
comparison of deleted and surviving posts on collection-time features,
and engagement-drift trajectories. *Expected challenge:* the ethics are
the design: once a post is deleted you must drop its content and keep
only the fact and date of deletion.
